Ask the body to help identify what it holds and how files are organised (series, registry refs, who held the file) before or after a request. A refusal to help is itself a ground of complaint.

Written request for recorded information. Land, buildings, planning and heritage records are usually environmental information, so ask for them under the EIR too: no cost limit, a presumption in favour of disclosure, and oral requests are valid.
rungs.note: 26FOI 103 answered 22 Sep: pointed to the Welsh Government.
rungs.cost: Free (copying costs only if they say so in advance)

rungs.why: Where the answer is 'not held', ask for the searches done: which registries, file plans, archives and off-site stores, which search terms, who searched, and whether files were transferred, destroyed or are held by another body. The ICO decides 'held' on the balance of probabilities, so a thin search is challengeable.
rungs.law: EIR reg 12(4)(a); FOIA s.1(1)(a); ICO guidance on whether information is held

rungs.why: Ask for the retention schedule that applied, the file plan entry, the disposal/destruction log, who authorised disposal and when, and any transfer to an archive. Altering or destroying records after a request is an offence.
rungs.law: FOIA s.46 Code of Practice (records management); FOIA s.77 / EIR reg 19

rungs.why: The family's own personal data, including notes, emails and file entries about him. It doesn't cover the deceased; their records need the other routes.
Ask the body to reconsider: the exemptions, the searches, the regime (EIR not FOIA), and any delay. This step is needed before the ICO will act.
rungs.law: FOIA s.45 Code of Practice; EIR reg 11

rungs.why: The body's own complaints procedure, for service failure: delay, ignored letters, lost files. It is needed before the Ombudsman.
Ask the Information Commissioner for a decision notice: on delay, on 'not held', on exemptions, or on whether the EIR apply. The ICO can order disclosure.

Appeal an ICO decision notice to the First-tier Tribunal (General Regulatory Chamber). Then, on a point of law and with permission, to the Upper Tribunal. No fee to appeal; costs only for unreasonable conduct.
rungs.law: FOIA s.57; GRC Rules 2009 r.22; TCEA 2007 s.11
rungs.cost: Free (no tribunal fee)

rungs.why: If the tribunal gets the law wrong, ask permission to appeal to the Upper Tribunal.
rungs.law: FOIA s.59; Tribunals, Courts and Enforcement Act 2007 s.11

rungs.why: Ask your Member of the Senedd, MP or councillor to raise the records question, or to table a written question. Members' enquiries often get files searched that a request did not.
rungs.law: Members' casework (no statute); Senedd written questions

rungs.why: For UK government bodies: maladministration complaints must be referred by an MP. They come after the body's own complaints process.
If a requested record was altered, blocked, erased, destroyed or concealed after the request to stop it being disclosed, report it to the Information Commission, which prosecutes this offence.
A formal letter setting out the claim and asking for the documents. Ignoring it has costs consequences in court.
For a public body's decision: the protocol letter, then a claim in the Administrative Court. The 3-month limit runs from the decision, so this rung has its own clock.
A court can order a controller to comply with a subject access request and award compensation.
Against someone who is not a party but holds documents, or who was mixed up in the wrongdoing: a court order to produce them.
rungs.law: CPR 31.17; Norwich Pharmacal v Customs and Excise [1974] AC 133

rungs.why: Against a body likely to be a party to a claim: a court order for documents before the claim is issued.
